I think it is better to put it in perspective for ppl fretting that their GPU is no longer going to be able to run games:

Is Turing Faster?

With both video cards operating nearly at the same frequency this creates an interesting scenario. We are basically looking at two video cards with similar clock speeds. We can estimate if GeForce RTX 2070’s Turing architecture might be faster than the previous Pascal architecture. It is important to realize there are more SM Units but less CUDA Cores (64 CUDA cores per SM versus 128 on Pascal) and Texture Units on GeForce RTX 2070 when compared to GeForce GTX 1080. In terms of GPU performance, this would mean slower performance on GeForce RTX 2070 if clock speed is the same. However, Turing is a new architecture. There are technically more SM Units, even if there are less CUDA Cores per SM. What we can then gather is if the architectural changes make up for the loss in overall CUDA Cores and Texture Units.
According to our testing the results all signs point to yes, the Turing architecture is definitely superior to, and faster than, the Pascal architecture at similar clock speeds. In all of our testing the MSI GeForce RTX 2070 GAMING Z consistently provided faster performance at 1440p and 4K compared to the MSI GeForce GTX 1080 GAMING X video card, despite having a CUDA Core and Texture Unit deficit, at the same clock speeds. text:
Thanks for the review and candid thoughts. My two cents is that the RTX 2070, 2080 and 2080 Ti are all very good products. As expected, each new RTX card can match and/or exceed the previous generation's card one step above. NVIDIA got this right as they always do. The problem is that they also match and/or exceed the previous generation's card price by a substantial amount at every level,  killing the value tiers everyone was used to throughout the GTX 9XX and 10XX series. Without that value, the only draws left are the Ray-Tracing and DLSS abilities and we have nothing yet to prove that those are worth the extra money. 

This leaves a huge opportunity IMHO for both AMD and Intel to draw competitively if they can accomplish one of two scenarios: 1. Offer the same performance tiers as the RTX cards only at a much lower price point thanks to the 7 nm process; or 2. Match the current RTX price points at each level but blow the RTX cards out of the water with far superior performance for the same price. Opportunity, however, doesn't equal guarantee. Remember that after much hype AMD's VEGA fell far short of beating the GTX series due to their having to fight off Intel on the CPU front and develop for the console market a tthe same time. Something had to give and the graphics division did. That's why everybody left the division. The same thing could happen again.  Intel is also distracted by fighting off AMD in the CPU market and might not be as prepared as everyone would hope to enter a three-way fight for the GPU market. We will all see this play out over 2019 and into 2020.
